R02-B-01: Experts who manage risk often speak of the public with weary patience. People, they observe, fear the wrong things. They worry about a nuclear plant that has never harmed anyone in the district while driving, without a second thought, along a road that kills several of their neighbours every year. They demand inquiries after a single dramatic accident and shrug at the steady toll of falls in the home. On this account the task of policy is to correct a problem of perception: to replace vivid fears with sober numbers, so that resources follow expected deaths rather than headlines. There is something to this, but less than its confidence suggests. When people are asked to describe what makes a hazard frightening, their answers are not random. Risks feel worse when they are imposed rather than chosen, when they could kill many people at once rather than a few at a time, when their effects are delayed or invisible, and when those who create them are not those who bear them. None of these features is captured by a count of expected fatalities, yet none of them is obviously foolish. A person who accepts the dangers of rock climbing but objects to a factory releasing an untested chemical into the river is not confused about arithmetic. She is drawing a distinction between a risk she has consented to and one that has been placed on her by others, and that distinction is a moral one that most legal systems also recognise. Seen this way, the gap between expert and lay rankings of hazards is partly a disagreement about what the question is. The expert asks how many people will die; the citizen asks, in addition, whether the arrangement that produces those deaths is fair, controllable and worthy of trust. To call the second question irrational is to settle a dispute about values by redescribing it as a dispute about facts. None of this makes dread a reliable guide. The features that make a hazard feel threatening can be manufactured by vivid reporting, and fear can drive choices that increase the very danger it is meant to avoid. If travellers abandon aircraft for cars after a well-publicised crash, they may exchange a small risk for a larger one without noticing the trade. The sensible response is neither to dismiss public fear as noise nor to treat it as a verdict. It is to take it apart: to ask which of its components reflect values that deserve a hearing in policy, and which reflect only the salience of a recent and alarming image.
R02-B-02: Few findings from the psychology of decision-making have travelled as far as the idea that too much choice is bad for us. The claim has a satisfying shape. It flatters the suspicion that modern abundance has not made people happier, and it offers a tidy remedy: fewer options, simpler shelves, shorter menus. Retailers have trimmed product lines in its name, and essayists have used it to diagnose a whole culture of anxious shoppers frozen before walls of nearly identical goods. Its appeal, in short, owes at least as much to its moral resonance as to the strength of the evidence on which it was originally built. The evidence, however, is less tidy than the slogan. A handful of striking early experiments suggested that people offered many options were less likely to choose at all, and less satisfied when they did. Later attempts to reproduce such effects produced a far more mixed picture: sometimes the effect appeared, sometimes it vanished, and sometimes larger assortments made people more likely to buy. A finding that reverses under slightly different conditions is not a law of human nature. It is a clue that the conditions themselves are doing the work. What might those conditions be? The more careful research points to a few. Large sets seem to burden people when they lack settled preferences in the domain, when the options differ along many dimensions that are hard to compare, when no option is marked as a sensible default, and when the decision feels consequential enough to invite later regret. A wine enthusiast choosing among forty bottles is browsing; a novice choosing among forty pension funds is drowning. The number of options is the same. What differs is whether the chooser has a way of sorting them, and therefore whether the abundance in front of him registers as an opportunity or as an accumulation of possible mistakes for which he alone will be answerable. This reframing matters because it changes the remedy. If abundance itself were the problem, the answer would be to cut. If the problem is the absence of structure, the answer is often to organise: to group options by the features people care about, to supply defaults that can be overridden, to let people narrow the field in stages. Cutting still has its place, particularly when most of the options are poor or nearly identical. But a policy of reduction applied everywhere would deprive the enthusiast of what she values in order to rescue the novice from a difficulty that better design could have removed.
R02-B-03: Ask people to estimate a quantity they do not know, after first asking whether it is higher or lower than some number, and their estimates will drift toward that number. The effect survives when participants have watched the number being produced at random, when they are told it is meaningless, and when they are paid for accuracy. It appears among amateurs and professionals alike, in guesses about the age of a building, the price of a house or a reasonable figure with which to open a negotiation. That arbitrary numbers can move consequential judgements is now one of the least disputed findings in the study of decision-making. Why they do so is more disputed, and the answer matters more than it first appears. The older explanation treats the anchor as a starting point. People begin at the number they are given and adjust away from it toward what seems plausible, but they stop too soon, at the first value that falls within a range they can accept. On this view anchoring is a failure of effort: the mind is a reluctant traveller who halts at the nearest acceptable station. The remedy follows naturally. Slow people down, ask them to think harder, give them reasons to care, and they will travel further from the anchor. A second explanation locates the problem earlier. When we are asked whether a building is older than, say, two hundred years, we do not merely note the number; we test it, and testing a hypothesis tends to mean searching for evidence that would make it true. We recall the building's worn stone and its old-fashioned windows, and these recollections, now freshly available, shape the estimate that follows. The anchor does not set a starting point so much as select the evidence. If this account is right, effort is no cure, because a more diligent search conducted in the same direction only gathers more of the same evidence. The two accounts are not exclusive. When people produce an anchor themselves, as when they start from a figure they already know and correct it for some difference, something like insufficient adjustment seems to occur, and in those cases encouraging effort does help. But for anchors supplied by others, which are the ones that negotiators, sellers and advocates supply deliberately, the evidence favours the selective account, and with it a different remedy: not to think harder about the number one has been handed but to think deliberately against it, by asking what would make it wrong.
R02-B-04: It is often said that overconfidence is the most pervasive of the biases, the one from which many of the others draw their strength. The claim is repeated so often that it is easy to miss how much it conceals. 'Overconfidence' names at least three different things, and they do not always travel together. Treating them as one has made the phenomenon seem both more universal and more mysterious than it is. The first is overestimation: believing that one has performed, or will perform, better than one actually does. The second is overplacement: believing that one is better than other people. The third, which receives less public attention, is overprecision: excessive certainty that one's beliefs are accurate, shown when people asked for a range they are ninety per cent sure contains some true value give ranges that contain it far less often than that. These sound like variations on a single vanity, but they come apart in revealing ways. On tasks that are easy, people tend to underestimate how well they have done, even as they place themselves above others; on tasks that are very hard, the pattern reverses, and many people will rate themselves below average at, say, juggling or composing verse while still overestimating their own scores. What explains such reversals is less a desire to think well of oneself than the way information is distributed. People usually know more about their own performance than about other people's, so their judgements of others are pulled toward a vague middle. When a task is hard, they sense that they did poorly, if not quite how poorly, but assume that others did less badly; when it is easy, the opposite. A good deal of what looks like ego, in other words, is a predictable consequence of reasoning from imperfect information about the people with whom one is being compared. Overprecision is different. It shows no comparable tendency to reverse, appearing on easy and hard questions, among novices and among specialists, and it is the form that does most harm in planning, where projects are budgeted against ranges too narrow to include what actually happens. It is also the form that most resists exhortation: telling forecasters to be humble rarely widens their intervals much. More promising are procedures that change the question, such as asking people to assign probabilities to several ranges in turn, so that the possibility of an outcome far from their best guess must be considered explicitly rather than waved away. The lesson is not that confidence is good or bad but that a single word has been doing the work of three, and that each of the three needs its own diagnosis.
R02-B-05: If biases are errors, it seems natural to suppose that teaching people about them should reduce them. Hence the many workshops in which managers, doctors and analysts are taken through a catalogue of the mind's failings, from anchoring to the sunk-cost fallacy, in the hope that knowing the names will help them avoid the traps. The hope is reasonable, and it is mostly disappointed. Participants usually leave such sessions able to define the biases and to spot them in descriptions of other people's reasoning. What they far less often do is reason differently when a fresh problem, dressed in unfamiliar clothes, arrives in their own work. Part of the difficulty is that biases rarely announce themselves. A textbook problem about sunk costs is labelled, at least implicitly, by the chapter in which it appears; a real decision about whether to keep funding a struggling project comes with no such label, and with colleagues, budgets and reputations attached. Recognising a pattern in a tidy example is a different skill from noticing it in a messy situation, and teaching the first does not automatically produce the second. There is also a subtler obstacle. People readily accept that biases exist and readily see them at work in others, while judging their own conclusions to be the products of careful thought. Instruction can even sharpen this asymmetry, supplying a vocabulary for diagnosing colleagues without unsettling one's own sense of seeing clearly. None of this shows that debiasing is hopeless. A few interventions built around repeated practice, varied examples and immediate feedback on one's own errors have produced improvements that outlasted the session, though how far they reach beyond the kinds of problem used in training remains uncertain. And there is a quieter strategy that sidesteps the question of individual reform altogether: changing the procedures within which decisions are made. A committee that collects independent estimates before discussion, or a review that requires someone to argue the case against a favoured plan, does not need its members to have become wiser. It builds the correction into the routine. The contrast is instructive. Approaches that rely on informing the individual treat bias as a kind of ignorance, curable by knowledge. Approaches that redesign procedures treat it as a standing feature of minds working under ordinary conditions, to be managed rather than eliminated. The second view is less flattering, but it fits the evidence better, and it has the practical merit of not depending on each person's ability to catch themselves in the act.
R02-B-06: Debates about intuition tend to fall into two camps that talk past each other. One camp collects cases in which experienced professionals, asked to explain a snap judgement, cannot say how they knew, and yet were right: the nurse who senses that a patient is deteriorating before the monitors register anything, the engineer who distrusts a design at a glance. The other camp collects cases in which confident experts did no better than simple formulas, or than chance, at predicting outcomes in their own fields. Each camp treats its own cases as the typical ones and the other camp's as curiosities. A way through the impasse begins by asking what intuition is. On the most plausible account it is recognition: the rapid matching of a present situation to patterns stored from earlier ones, which brings with it a sense of what is likely to happen next and of what to do. Recognition of this kind can be only as good as the patterns it has learned, and patterns can be learned only where two conditions hold. The environment must contain regularities that link cues to outcomes, and the person must have had extensive practice with feedback quick and clear enough to reveal whether a judgement was right. A ward where patients either recover or worsen within hours satisfies both conditions. A market in which prices reflect the guesses of many other participants, and in which the consequences of a choice emerge slowly and mixed with luck, satisfies neither very well. This account explains why both camps can find their cases. It also yields a less comfortable conclusion. The feeling of knowing that accompanies intuition is produced in the same way whether or not the underlying patterns are valid. A forecaster who has spent years in an environment with little regularity can feel as sure as a nurse, because confidence grows with familiarity and with the coherence of the story one can tell, not with accuracy. Subjective certainty therefore tells us almost nothing about whether to trust a judgement. What tells us something is the environment in which the judgement was learned. The practical upshot is not that intuition should be confined to a list of approved professions. The same expert may work in a high-validity environment for some tasks and a low-validity one for others. A clinician may become very good at judging, within minutes, whether a patient needs urgent attention, while long-range predictions about the same patient's recovery, whose outcomes arrive years later and are shaped by many intervening events, remain little better than guesses. The question to ask of any intuition, then, is not who holds it or how firmly, but whether the conditions for learning it were ever present.
R02-B-07: The demonstration is by now familiar. Two groups are offered the same treatment, described in two ways: to one group as leaving ninety in a hundred patients alive after a year, to the other as seeing ten in a hundred die. The numbers are identical, yet the first description reliably attracts more support than the second. Since the treatment does not differ, the argument runs, a rational agent should not respond to the difference in wording, and the fact that people do respond is evidence that their preferences are shaped by presentation rather than substance. The principle appealed to, that logically equivalent descriptions should produce the same choice, has seemed so obvious that few have thought it needed defending. Yet the principle is less obvious than it looks once we remember that descriptions do not fall from the sky. Somebody chooses them, and the choice is rarely arbitrary. A doctor who believes a treatment is worth trying tends, without any intent to manipulate, to speak of the patients it saves; a doctor with doubts more naturally mentions those it fails. Speakers also tend to describe a quantity in terms of the reference point from which it has moved: a glass that was full and has been partly drunk is more often called half empty than half full. If such regularities hold, then the frame carries information that the bare numbers do not, and a listener who draws an inference from it is not being swayed by mere wording. She is reading what the speaker's choice of words reveals, much as she would read an emphasis or a pause. On this view, many framing effects are better described as sensitivity to implicit information than as failures of logic, and the experimenter who insists on equivalence has mistaken the logic of sentences for the logic of conversation. The equivalence holds between the propositions; it does not hold between the acts of uttering them, because those acts tell the hearer different things about the speaker. Participants who bring their ordinary conversational competence into the laboratory are, in a sense, being too reasonable for the experiment's purposes. This rehabilitation should not be pushed too far. When experiments go to some lengths to make the frame visibly arbitrary, for example by assigning descriptions by an evident coin toss or by presenting both descriptions together, the inference from frame to speaker has nothing to work on, and a rational participant should set it aside. Effects in such conditions are often smaller, which is what the information account predicts, but they do not always vanish. Some residue seems to reflect the plain pull of words such as 'die' and 'lose', a reaction that would survive any amount of reflection about speakers. The information account explains a good deal of the phenomenon; it does not explain all of it. What follows is a more discriminating verdict than either side usually offers. Whether responsiveness to a frame is a lapse depends on whether, in the situation at hand, the frame was a signal. Outside the laboratory it usually is, which is why habits formed in conversation are worth having. The danger lies precisely in that usefulness. A listener who reasonably treats frames as informative can be exploited by a speaker who knows the convention and chooses a frame to suggest a recommendation he would not dare to state outright. The fault in such cases lies less with the listener's inference than with the speaker's abuse of a norm that ordinarily makes the inference sound.
R02-B-08: For several decades one research tradition in psychology has proceeded by a simple method. Set people a problem whose correct answer is fixed by logic or probability theory, record the ways in which their answers depart from it, and infer from the pattern of departures the shortcuts the mind must be using. The method has been extraordinarily productive. It has yielded a catalogue of systematic errors, and with it a picture of human judgement as a set of serviceable but crude rules of thumb that fail predictably whenever a problem is constructed to expose them. That picture has travelled well beyond psychology, into economics, law and medicine, where it is now invoked to justify the design of forms, defaults and warnings meant to protect people from their own shortcuts. A rival tradition objects not to the findings but to the frame. A rule of thumb, it argues, can be judged only against the environment in which it is used, and the problems of the laboratory are often unlike the environments in which human judgement developed and in which it is mostly exercised. More provocatively, it points out that simple rules can outperform elaborate ones. When a decision must be made from a small sample in a noisy world, a model that weighs many cues carefully will fit the data at hand closely, including its accidents, and will then predict new cases worse than a rule that attends to one or two strong cues and ignores the rest. Ignoring information, which the first tradition tends to read as a symptom of limited capacity, can on this account be a source of accuracy. The point is sound, and it is worth seeing why it does not abandon the idea of a norm. The advantage of the simple rule is itself a result of statistical theory: it accepts a little systematic error in exchange for a large reduction in sensitivity to noise, and in small, noisy samples that exchange is often a good one. To praise frugal heuristics on these grounds is not to reject normative standards but to replace one standard, agreement with a probabilistic calculation on a fully specified problem, with another, accuracy in predicting cases one has not yet seen. That second standard is arguably the one that matters for creatures who must act on incomplete information. Where the rival tradition overreaches is in moving from what heuristics can do to what people actually do. To show that a rule performs well in some environments is not to show that people use it in those environments and abandon it in others. That further claim, that minds select their tools to suit the structure of the task, is an empirical hypothesis, and the evidence for it is uneven. People sometimes apply a rule where it serves them and sometimes carry it into settings where it misleads, and modern life supplies many settings, from the interpretation of medical test results to the assessment of financial risk, that resemble the laboratory more than the forest or the village market. The disagreement, then, is narrower than its polemics suggest. Both traditions accept that judgement relies on shortcuts, and both, when pressed, accept that a shortcut can be good or bad depending on where it is used. What separates them is a question that neither has fully answered: how well people match their methods to their circumstances. Answering it requires studying environments as carefully as minds, which neither tradition, in its more confident moments, has been much inclined to do.
